Hrithik's cough had started in the week the dairy cooperative in Anand launched its new billing system. He was the youngest person in the IT room and the only one who really understood the software, so every farmer's complaint came to him.
'Go to the clinic,' Zeenat said in the first week. 'After launch,' he said. In the third week she said it again. 'After the audit.' Each time, the thought of a doctor saying something bad made his stomach turn, and the project gave him a reason not to go.
By the sixth week he was coughing through calls and waking at night. When he finally went, the doctor at the town hospital asked why he hadn't come earlier, ordered tests, and said treatment would now take longer than it might have. Hrithik sat on the bench outside holding the prescription, feeling foolish and tired.
Zeenat was waiting by the gate. She didn't say 'I told you.' She just handed him tea.

qa.q: What did Hrithik say the first time Zeenat told him to go?
Why did Hrithik keep postponing the clinic?
qa.a: He was afraid of hearing bad news, and the busy project gave him an excuse that felt safe.

qa.q: What could Hrithik have done in the first week?
qa.a: Booked a short visit despite the launch, or asked a colleague to cover calls for an hour, since the cough kept going.

qa.q: What is it like for Zeenat to watch the weeks pass?
qa.a: Zeenat is worried and keeps nudging, then chooses kindness over blame when he finally goes.

grounding: Shows a young worker, busy and afraid of bad news, postponing a check-up for weeks, which delays treatment and adds stress.

subtype: Approach: avoid the appointment hoping it will pass [Pitfall]
passage:
Dalia's right wrist had ached since spring, when her design studio in Vancouver took on a huge rebrand. Some mornings she couldn't hold her coffee cup without wincing.
Her flatmate Bao noticed her shaking out her hand at dinner. 'Have you seen someone?'
'After the deadline.'
The deadline moved twice. Dalia kept a wrist brace in her bag and a quiet dread in her chest. If a doctor told her to stop drawing, what would she do? Not knowing felt safer than knowing.
Nine weeks later the pain woke her at night. Bao sat with her while she booked a clinic slot for the next morning. The doctor examined her wrist, asked why she had waited so long, and referred her to a physiotherapist, saying recovery would probably take longer now than if she'd come in sooner.
Walking home, Dalia said, 'I was scared of losing my job. I nearly wrecked my wrist for it.'
'Yes,' Bao said. 'Let's not do that again.'

qa.q: When did Dalia say she would see someone?
Why did Dalia keep avoiding the doctor?
qa.a: She was frightened a doctor would tell her to stop drawing, so not knowing felt safer.

qa.q: What could Dalia have done in spring instead?
qa.a: Seen a doctor early while still working, and asked the studio for help spreading the drawing load.

qa.q: What was it like for Bao to watch this?
qa.a: Bao noticed the pain early and asked gently, then stayed with Dalia when it got worse, probably worried the whole time.

grounding: Shows a young worker, busy and afraid of bad news, postponing a check-up for weeks until the delay makes recovery longer.
